transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-01-10 15:00 PST
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Cheng (Redwood AE), Marco Rinaldi (Redwood SE), Naomi Park (Redwood SE), Priya Narang (Elmwood CISO), Daniel Moss (Elmwood Cloud Architect), Leah Ortiz (Elmwood Head of Compliance), Omar Khalid (Elmwood DevOps)

[00:00] Alyssa: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we appreciate you taking the time. I'm Alyssa Cheng from Redwood, and with me are Marco and Naomi. Today's goal is a security and network deep dive for the Private VPC / on-prem deployment you asked about.
[00:12] Priya: Thanks, Alyssa. We want to make sure we cover ingress/egress, firewall rules, how control plane communicates, and the KMS options. Also SOC 2 and ISO evidence - what you can provide.
[00:22] Marco: Great. Quick agenda - we'll go over deployment modes, control plane connectivity options (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), required outbound endpoints, host-level firewalling recommendations, and then tie it back to compliance artifacts. I'll try to show a small diagram.
[00:35] Daniel: Awesome. We're primarily interested in a customer-managed VPC with an option to air-gap certain environments. We have strict egress controls via a corporate proxy and most egress must go through a proxy appliance.
[00:46] Naomi: Noted. We support control plane using two patterns: a) PrivateLink into Redwood control plane, or b) pinned control plane endpoints over an allow-listed set of IPs, optionally tunneled via customer-managed NAT or forward proxies. Both can be used with Private deployments.
[01:00] Leah: A quick question - for audit logs, do you push logs back to our S3 or do we pull them? We need immutable logs retained for 7 years for some regs.
[01:08] Marco: Current pattern is push-based - we can ship logs to customer-owned S3 buckets or to their SIEM via syslog/forwarder. We also provide an audit export.
[01:20] Priya: And encryption - do you support customer-managed keys (CMK) in our KMS / HSM? We can't have Redwood manage keys for certain data classes.
[01:28] Naomi: Yes, we support a bring-your-own-key flow. For hosted objects and model artifacts we can encrypt with your KMS keys; for on-prem deployments the HSM integration is available via PKCS#11 or cloud HSM interfaces. There may be some operations around key policy changes we need to coordinate on.
[01:40] Omar: Quick nit - do you require any outbound access to telemetry or usage endpoints? Our proxy blocks almost everything by default.
[01:46] Marco: We do have telemetry and metrics endpoints - optional by default for compliance sensitive installs. If blocked, some observability features will be limited. For Private deployments, we can disable telemetry or route it over your proxy to allowed endpoints. The minimal outbound list includes: auth.redwood.example.com, storage.redwood.example.com, container-registry.redwood.example.com - those are examples, we'll provide a precise list.
[02:10] Daniel: About network isolation - how do you separate workloads? We run multiple tenants and need strong segmentation between production and dev.
[02:18] Naomi: We recommend separate subnets per workload with security groups and host-level policies. For container hosts we use OS-level egress rules and iptables or nftables for host-level firewalling, plus VPC security groups for cloud. For on-prem you can use VLAN segmentation and host firewall policies. Also we can pin KV cache nodes to isolated subnets to avoid cross-tenant leaks.
[02:40] Priya: Can you walk through the control plane flow again? I want to understand inbound and outbound - especially ingress from our side.
[02:48] Marco: Sure. Control plane traffic is primarily outbound from customer network to Redwood control endpoints - so no inbound holes are required on your firewall for the runtime. For PrivateLink, you create an interface VPC endpoint that points to our service, which stays within the AWS network; control plane comms then traverse AWS backbone. For peering, it's routed via peering connections - both avoid public internet egress.
[03:10] Priya: For on-prem air-gapped, is there an offline bundle or do you require periodic connections?
[03:16] Naomi: We provide an on-prem package that can be deployed air-gapped; however for model updates or security patches a secure update process exists where packages are signed and can be transferred via secure media. If you need periodic telemetry or usage, we can schedule push intervals via an approved egress channel.
[03:30] Leah: From a compliance perspective, we need evidence of separation and role-based access. How does Redwood map SSO groups to RBAC?
[03:38] Marco: We integrate with SAML/SSO providers (Okta, Azure AD) and can map SAML attributes/groups to Redwood roles. For Private installs we can configure SCIM or on-prem group syncs. We also support fine-grained RBAC with audit trails for role changes.
[03:55] Daniel: Are audit logs write-once? We need tamper-evident logs.
[03:59] Naomi: Logs can be pushed to your write-once S3 with object lock enabled or to WORM-compliant storage. We also support pushing to your SIEM where retention policies can be enforced. Internally we keep an append-only audit store but for compliance, customer-managed storage is recommended.
[04:20] Priya: On firewalling - do you recommend NACLs in addition to security groups? We're worried about lateral movement.
[04:27] Marco: Yes, NACLs for subnet-level stateless filtering plus security groups on instances for stateful filtering is a common pattern. For on-prem, VLANs + host-level iptables/nft rules and host-based IDS can be layered. We also recommend host-level process isolation (container runtime seccomp) particularly for components that handle customer data.
[04:48] Omar: What about egress restrictions for model files? We can't allow model downloads to arbitrary places.
[04:53] Naomi: Model artifacts are stored in customer-owned storage if you choose private mode, and access is controlled by the runtime. We can restrict model pull to internal networks and ensure that runtime nodes only pull from authorized registries. For hosted models, we can also provide restricted image registries or proxying through your proxied nat gateway.
[05:10] Leah: Any third-party pen tests or SOC2 scope details you can share?
[05:15] Alyssa: We'll share our SOC 2 Type II report and the latest ISO attestation under NDA via the secure link. Naomi will upload them to the shared folder. We do annual pen tests and can provide summaries; detailed pen test reports are typically shared under NDA.
[05:30] Priya: Great. Another question - do you support customer-managed DNS or do you require Redwood to own certain DNS records for control endpoints?
[05:38] Marco: You can keep control over DNS. For PrivateLink we create an endpoint and you can map it to a private hosted zone. For peering, your internal DNS can resolve our internal control plane addresses. We'll avoid requiring public DNS changes for Private deployments.
[05:55] Daniel: Anything special about firewall rules for health checks/heartbeats? We need ports.
[06:00] Naomi: Heartbeats are outbound on HTTPS over port 443 typically. We'll provide a list of ports, but the recommendation is to allow outbound 443 to the control plane endpoints. For on-prem health checks between nodes, we use internal ports for kube / runtime communication, which stay inside the VPC or vlan.
[06:20] Priya: Will you provide terraform examples for network setup?
[06:23] Alyssa: Yes - we'll share sample terraform modules for subnets, security groups, and PrivateLink endpoints. That's one of the action items.
[06:30] Marco: Also quick note on keys - for CMK usage we require an IAM role assumption pattern or HSM integration. On AWS, you can grant the Redwood service principal a key usage policy scoped to the resources it needs. We can also support envelope encryption where your KMS only unwraps data keys.
[06:50] Omar: For HSM - do you have integrations with YubiHSM or HashiCorp Vault?
[06:55] Naomi: We have documented integrations for cloud HSMs (AWS CloudHSM) and PKCS#11 compatible HSMs. For Vault, we can tap into the Transit engine for key operations. Some engineering work is required for secret rotation flows; we'll provide a reference design.
[07:10] Leah: On retention of audit logs, can we set retention at the per-log type level? We need 7 years for access logs, 1 year for debug.
[07:18] Marco: Absolutely, if logs land in your SIEM or S3 you control lifecycle policies. We can tag logs by type so retention policies can be applied.
[07:28] Priya: Are there any features that won't work if we block all outbound except a handful of endpoints?
[07:34] Naomi: Streaming telemetry and live usage dashboards will be limited. Also for container image pulls we need access to your private registry or to allowlist our registry endpoints. Model updater services may require outbound access unless you opt for offline bundles.
[07:50] Daniel: Regarding network performance - do you have recommendations for throughput-sensitive workloads?
[07:56] Marco: Yes: place runtime nodes in subnets with enhanced networking, use placement groups for reduced latency on cloud, and for on-prem ensure NIC teaming and jumbo frames if large token throughput is expected. Also prefer local NVMe for KV cache to reduce latency.
[08:20] Leah: Can you describe the incident response handoff process? We need to know how security events are escalated.
[08:27] Alyssa: We have a documented incident response playbook. For Private customers we integrate with your pager or Ticketing system. We will provide SLA'ed notification times in the enterprise contract and include a point of contact for security incidents. Naomi will attach a redacted runbook.
[08:46] Priya: About compliance scope - is the control plane included in SOC2 scope when we run Private?
[08:52] Naomi: Control plane components that process metadata are included; however, for Private deployments where the control plane is in your VPC, we can scope parts under customer responsibility. We'll provide the detailed responsibility matrix showing which controls Redwood maintains and which are customer-managed.
[09:12] Daniel: One more - do you support mutual TLS for node-to-control-plane?
[09:16] Marco: Yes, mTLS is supported for node connections, and we can present client certs that are rotated periodically. That's recommended for on-prem setups to ensure only authorized nodes can talk to control plane.
[09:30] Leah: Okay, let's recap next steps - Alyssa do you want to do the recap?
[09:34] Alyssa: Sure. We'll: 1) Share VPC/network diagram + terraform module (Alyssa), 2) Naomi to upload SOC 2/ISO attestation and pen test summary, 3) Marco will provide firewall/security group templates and NACL examples, 4) Elmwood (Daniel) will send our proxy egress rules and IPs, 5) schedule network walkthrough next week.
[09:58] Priya: Yep that's right. Please mark SOC docs as NDA only.
[10:02] Alyssa: Absolutely. We'll send a secure link.
[10:06] Daniel: Thanks, team. We'll review the docs and come back with any gaps.
[10:10] Omar: One small point - can you include a sample iptables snippet for blocking metadata service from workloads? We have a known issue in our fleet.
[10:18] Marco: We'll include that in the templates - blocking 169.254.169.254 at host level with iptables is a common pattern, and we have a hardened snippet.
[10:30] Leah: Thanks everyone.
[10:33] Alyssa: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
